title: Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoints now support KV cache aware routing
abstract: Today, Amazon SageMaker AI introduces KV cache-aware routing (KV-aware routing), a new routing strategy for real-time endpoints. It uses the cache state that the model container reports. It sends each request to an instance that already holds a long cached match for its prompt and isn’t too busy. It’s for teams that serve large language models (LLMs) with multi-turn conversations, long shared prompts, or heavy load. You turn it on in two places: add one environment variable to your model so the container reports its cache contents, and set RoutingStrategy to KV_AWARE in the endpoint configuration. Your clients call the endpoint with the same APIs as before. Here’s the problem it solves: LLM applications such as chat assistants, Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG), and agents with long system prompts send many requests that start with the same text. A model keeps the work it did on a prompt in GPU memory, the KV cache, and skips that work when the same start reaches the same instance again. In part 1 of this series , we introduced prefix-aware routing for Amazon SageMaker AI, which sends requests that start the same way to the same instance. Prefix-aware routing infers where a prefix is cached from the request alone, so it can’t tell when an instance has evicted that cache. Prefix-aware routing picks an instance from the request alone. It hashes the start of the request, up to the PrefixLength you configure (bytes of the InvokeEndpoint payload, or characters of the message text for the OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions API), and sends requests that start the same way to the same instance. It never sees what an instance actually has cached. This works well when every request starts with the same shared text, and less well in two cases: The cache on an instance changes over time. An instance evicts older KV cache entries when its GPU memory fills up, but the router keeps sending matching requests there as if the cache were still warm. A conversation starts out short. In a multi-turn chat, each turn adds to the history. While the request is still shorter than PrefixLength , every new turn changes the text the router hashes, so the next turn can land on a different instance than the one that cached the earlier turns. The turns of a conversation stay on one instance only after the request grows past PrefixLength . In this post, we explain how KV-aware routing works, when to use it, and how to enable, invoke, and verify it on single model endpoints and inference component endpoints. How KV-aware routing works KV-aware routing has three parts: the model container reports what it has cached, SageMaker AI keeps a managed cache index of that state for the endpoint, and the endpoint uses the index to choose an instance for each request. When you turn events on with SM_VLLM_KV_EVENTS_CONFIG , the container publishes a KV cache event each time it stores or evicts cache entries, and SageMaker AI uses these events to keep the index current. The index holds only pointers: one-way, truncated hashes of cached content, each mapped to the instance or inference component copy that holds it. It never stores prompts, token IDs, request payloads, or KV tensors. When a request arrives, the endpoint tokenizes the prompt and looks up the tokens in the index. The index returns the instances or inference component copies that hold part of the prompt in their cache, and how much of it each one holds. For example, if instance A holds the cached start of a conversation, the next turn of that conversation goes to A. Because the index matches on tokens rather than a fixed number of bytes, a multi-turn history can match in full as it grows. A request that shares only part of its prompt still goes to the instance with the longest match. The endpoint then picks among these candidates by weighing how much of the prompt each one has cached against how busy it is. A candidate that is too busy is skipped, so if the instance with the longest match is busy, the reques

title: Govern and discover records with common metadata in AWS Agent Registry
abstract: As organizations build more agents, Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers and skills, they need a consistent way to describe, govern, and find them. AWS Agent Registry provides a catalog for registering, approving, and discovering these resources and custom records. Each record carries a name, a description, a protocol descriptor, and an approval status. However, every organization has attributes and facts that it wants to track, and some are unique to that organization, such as its business units, resource owners, risk classifications, and development environments. Organizations want one common definition for each of these attributes, and they want every agent, MCP server, and skill in the registry to carry these facts. Until now, organizations had no way to define these facts in AWS Agent Registry and store them on each record. Custom metadata schemas are now available in AWS Agent Registry. A custom metadata schema is a set of organization-defined key-value pairs that records in an AWS Agent Registry carry. An administrator defines the schema and applies it to the registry, and all records within the registry must then adhere to the schema. When publishers create or submit records, they supply values for the fields specified in the applicable schema, and AWS Agent Registry validates those values against the schema set by the admin. Approvers can rely on the validated values when reviewing a record, and consumers and agents can use them to discover and filter records. Administrators, publishers, security and governance teams, approvers, consumers, and agents all work from a shared set of facts to govern, discover, and understand the resources in their agentic fleet. In this post, we follow the AnyCompany organization publishing an MCP server with custom schema definition, enriching that record, and making it available for discovery by humans or agents. We use an MCP server as the example, but the same steps apply to other record types. How custom metadata works With custom metadata, an organization can use standardized vocabulary for describing its resources. The registry administrator defines the custom metadata schema : field names, types, allowed values, and whether each field is required or optional. The registry enforces the schema on every record, so a field such as environment has the same name and the same allowed values whichever team publishes the record. The schema has common attributes that apply to every record type, and you can add dedicated fields that only apply to specific record types. Each field is Text, Enum, URL, or Boolean. When a record is created or updated, the registry validates the custom metadata against the schema set up by the admin. If a record is created without any custom metadata, AWS Agent Registry saves it as NON_COMPLIANT . A team can save work in progress this way, but it can’t submit the record for approval until it has the required fields and values. If a record includes custom metadata with an unknown field, a missing required field, or an invalid value, AWS Agent Registry rejects it with a ValidationException . GetRegistryRecord returns the record’s custom metadata values and its compliance status. ( COMPLIANT means that the values match the administrator’s schema. It is not an approval. The approvers make that decision.) Discovery APIs also allow filtering records based on custom attributes. What custom metadata makes possible Because teams can describe the AWS Agent Registry records with the same fields and values, the registry can support and scale governance and compliance. Ownership and operations Fields such as environment ( prod , staging , or dev ), businessUnit , ownerTeam , supportContact , and costCenter record where a resource runs, who is responsible for it, and who pays for it. A configuration management database (CMDB) ID links the record to your existing inventory, and a support-tier field sets expectations for anyone who depends on the resource. Security and complianc

title: Secure OAuth patterns for Snowflake Cortex AI through Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
abstract: Enterprises today need a clear way to extend their authentication and authorization controls into the agentic layer, often requiring either broad service account permissions or custom-built auth integrations that add operational overhead. When an AI agent running on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore (a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model) needs to call the Snowflake-managed MCP server (which exposes Snowflake Cortex Agents as one of its tool types) through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), the first question enterprises must answer is: how does the agent authenticate? In this post, we walk through three Open Authorization (OAuth) configurations we tested on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity , a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore: Snowflake OAuth (per-user, no external Identity Provider, or IdP), three-legged OAuth with a third-party Identity Provider (corporate single sign-on, or SSO), and two-legged OAuth with a third-party Identity Provider (shared service user). Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity also supports an on-behalf-of (OBO) grant (TOKEN_EXCHANGE) that delivers per-user identity for unattended workloads without a consent prompt. We focus on the three configurations we tested end-to-end, flagging where OBO fits as we go. By the end, you will be able to identify which pattern suits your enterprise scenario. Solution overview Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway , a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, connects AI agents to external tool providers through MCP server targets. It targets the Snowflake-managed MCP server, which surfaces Cortex Search and Cortex Analyst as MCP tools that an MCP-aware client can discover and invoke. Rather than acting as a wrapper, the Gateway aggregates the capabilities of its configured targets into a single unified catalog, which it presents to the agent as one tools/list response. The core focus of this post is the outbound authentication for Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway: how it obtains and presents OAuth tokens to the Snowflake-managed MCP server. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity acts as the credential broker: the Gateway obtains a workload token by calling GetWorkloadAccessTokenForJWT (because the Gateway uses JSON Web Token (JWT) inbound authentication), then calls GetResourceOauth2Token against the configured provider. AgentCore Identity owns the token vault, the token refresh, and the user-to-token binding, and it fetches, caches, and refreshes tokens automatically. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity supports three OAuth configurations spanning two grant types (authorization_code and client_credentials): Snowflake OAuth : Snowflake acts as its own OAuth authorization server. Each user authenticates directly to Snowflake through the Authorization Code grant (3LO). No external identity provider is needed. Three-legged OAuth using a third-party Identity Provider: Users authenticate through corporate SSO with the Authorization Code grant. Snowflake trusts IdP-issued JSON Web Tokens (JWTs) through its External OAuth security integration. Two-legged OAuth pattern using a third-party IdP: A shared service user authenticates through the client_credentials grant of the IdP. No user interaction or consent is required, which is ideal for machine-to-machine workloads. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity also offers an API-key credential provider (which supports Snowflake Programmatic Access Tokens). We focus on OAuth here for per-user attribution and automatic token refresh. Each configuration uses a credential provider in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity (CustomOauth2, OktaOauth2, or MicrosoftOauth2) and a corresponding security integration on the Snowflake side. Note: We tested these patterns with the Snowflake-managed MCP server using Okta and Microsoft Entra ID. Patterns 2 and 3 (external IdP) follow standard OAuth flows, so they can extend to other OAuth-protected MCP servers, but validate the token claims, scopes, and audience settings for you

title: Announcing AI data preparation capabilities in Amazon SageMaker: Build high-quality datasets for model development workflows
abstract: Teams that ship generative AI to production know that a model is only as good as its data. That is why preparing high-quality training and evaluation data comes first. Fine-tuning an open-weight model, running reinforcement learning, or building an evaluation suite all depend on data that is accurate, well-labeled, and representative of your task. For narrow, well-defined tasks, a smaller model customized on clean, task-specific data can often match or exceed the accuracy of a larger general-purpose model prompted into shape, at a lower cost per inference. In practice, though, preparing that data is often the slowest part of the project. Labeled examples are scarce or expensive, and privacy rules limit what you can use. Quality problems such as duplicates, label noise, and answer leakage go unnoticed until a training run disappoints, and every training technique expects data in its own format. As a result, data scientists spend weeks wrangling data instead of building models. Today, we’re expanding Amazon SageMaker AI with new AI data preparation capabilities for model development workflows. You can generate synthetic examples, assess and improve existing datasets, and bring expert feedback into the process through Python SDK APIs and the AWS AI-ML agent skill. You work in your notebook or IDE, with specifications and code that you can inspect and change. Prepare data without hand-building pipelines With AI Data Preparation capabilities, you don’t need to stitch together labeling tools, generation scripts, and validation jobs. Each capability is a standalone building block. You can use one of them on its own or chain them together according to the workflow you want. Auto-labeling: Label data at scale from an unlabeled dataset, a small labeled seed set, or no labels at all. Built-in task types include classification, named entity recognition, extractive question answering, ordinal rating, and summarization, and you can define custom tasks. You describe the task in a short labeling spec, which is validated against your own examples before the full dataset is labeled. For tasks with a fixed set of possible answers, such as classification, named entity recognition, and extractive question answering, a jury of several models labels each row, and their level of agreement becomes that row’s confidence score. Human review: Rows below your confidence threshold go to a review queue in Amazon SageMaker Studio, which uses the open-source Label Studio Community Edition. Outside subject matter experts can access the review app through the link in the partner app box in SageMaker Studio. Reviewer corrections feed back into auto-labeling, and you can generate consensus metrics and labeling reports. Synthetic data generation: Generate training, evaluation, and test data from a specification. You can ground the output in your own seed data and documents, and the service generates a code-based data generation pipeline that you can review, modify, reuse, and scale. Data quality evaluation: Check datasets against your own business rules, built-in metrics, and LLM-as-a-judge metrics. Find duplicates and near-duplicates, and surface issues you didn’t think to check for, such as label noise or answer leakage. Data transformation: Clean and reshape data for your target training technique. Describe the change in plain language and have the code generated for you, use built-in operations such as dedupe, merge, split, and filter, or run your own Python at scale. You work wherever you already work. Use the SageMaker Python SDK directly or provide your coding agent the AI-ML skill in the agent toolkit and let your agent invoke the APIs according to established data science best practices. Describe what you need, and the agent selects and runs the right capability in SageMaker Studio JupyterLab, Kiro, or your local IDE with your coding assistant of choice. title: Getting AI out of the demo and into businesses globally
abstract: AWS Forward Deployed Engineering is now available in 15 countries including U.S., Mexico, Brazil, Canada, Australia, Singapore, India, South Korea, Japan, UK, Germany, Netherlands, France, Sweden, and Saudi Arabia for commercial and public sector customers; and powered by dozens of built in production-ready accelerators. Every enterprise I talk to has built something with AI that works. A prototype that reads a claim. An agent that resolves a card dispute. A model that answers a customer question in seconds. The prototype works. The demo impresses stakeholders. Then the organization tries to put it into production, and the real problems begin. Production data is messier than the test set. Auditors want to know why the agent made each decision. Volume grows from a pilot group to the whole company. The rules that matter most turn out to live in people’s heads. None of these are model problems. They’re business problems, and they decide whether AI ever pays off. The stretch from demo to production is the last mile, where most AI stalls. It’s also where our teams spend their time. We launched AWS Forward Deployed Engineering (FDE) in June to close that gap. Since then, we’ve worked through these problems with commercial and public sector customers in financial services, healthcare, sports, media, retail, and more. Here’s what we’ve learned, and how it shaped what we built. The problem has three layers Model providers, cloud providers, and consulting firms are all embedding engineers with customers. At AWS FDE, we measure success by what remains after our engineers leave: a foundation your team owns, workflows that keep learning, and governance you can trust. Across customers, the hardest problems show up in three layers: the foundation, the workflows, and governance. Each one is harder than it looks, and each one builds on the one before it. That holds whether you’re starting fresh or building on existing systems. On a greenfield build, you can move fast, but there’s no foundation to stand on yet. On a brownfield system, agents must work within decades of data, rules, and integrations. Layer one: A foundation that compounds Before an agent can do useful work at scale, it needs a foundation: identity, security, context, governance, and operational controls. That foundation must be production-ready from day one and shared by every use case that follows. Context is often the biggest gap. Most customers have data spread across systems and no common ontology, the shared model of how the business works that agents need to reason over. Without a shared foundation, the second pilot costs nearly as much as the first. Integrations get rebuilt, and lessons fail to carry forward. Most organizations reach a point where they stop and build the foundation first, so each new use case starts from what the last one built instead of from scratch. We call this the AI reset. Samsung Life Insurance had four affiliates, each building its own AI point solutions from scratch. In 45 days, the FDE team built a governed agentic platform with a single control plane and compliance built in. New agents now deploy through registration and policy assignment instead of a rebuild. Layer two: Automating workflows Next is the work itself: High-volume, rule-heavy processes such as claims processing, know your customer (KYC) reviews, card disputes, loan origination, invoice reconciliation, permitting, and customer service. This is where AI can deliver immediate and measurable outcomes. The payoff is fast, but the knowledge that drives these processes rarely lives in a system. It lives with the people who do the work. The hard part isn’t automation itself. It is uncovering the business rules behind each decision. When an invoice and a purchase order disagree, which record wins? abstract: The challenges and decisions behind AI Discover’s intelligence layer By Varun Khaitan , Peng Ren , Gary Tang , Itay Teller , Atif Faheem , Nipun Kumar , Donnie DeBoer , Eduardo Lundgren , Matteo Rinaldi , Raghav Bakshi We recently introduced AI Discover , a new tab in our TV app where a small group of members can try new ways to find something to watch. For years, our recommendations have worked in the background, inferring what a member might enjoy from their viewing history. AI Discover moves from that silent ranking toward steerable discovery. A member picks a theme, say “Quick Watches,” and gets a row of matching titles, a short note on why they fit and a few narrower themes to try next. From there, they can keep narrowing, head somewhere new or tune what they see. Building AI Discover raised a question many teams will recognize: how do you deliver a better member experience with generative AI on TV without sacrificing speed, reliability or safety? Our answer is a new intelligence layer, the agent harness behind AI Discover. For each request, it decides how to combine LLMs with our recommendation systems. It builds on years of work understanding what members enjoy, and on our recent work applying LLMs to recommendations and generative experiences. The layer itself plans each request, runs it across those systems, serves the result and evaluates it offline. This post covers the challenges we designed for and the key decisions we made along the way. Why an intelligence layer? Every Netflix page combines recommendations with rules. We pick titles a member may enjoy, and eligibility, maturity and safety rules decide what can appear. An experience built on LLMs needs the same rules, plus code that decides when to call an LLM and how to handle its output. That code is called an agent harness, and it’s the core of our intelligence layer. The simplest implementation hands the entire request to an LLM and lets it pick the titles, write the labels and decide what happens next. However, that leaves us relying on probabilistic output where we need governed results, because every turn in AI Discover ends on a screen in someone’s living room. At our scale, even rare failures happen many times a day. A member sees every slow call, unavailable title or off-brand line. Seven challenges shaped our design: Fitting LLMs into a product and architecture designed without them. Traditional recommenders rank titles based on past behavior. LLMs can do more: understand what a member is asking for and plan how to respond. Our existing experience would leave most of that unused. Keeping recommendations grounded. Every pick must be a real, available title from our changing catalog. Retrieval and rankers work in tandem with LLMs to choose titles that fit the member’s taste and intent. Working with slow, unpredictable LLMs. LLM calls are the slowest and most expensive part of the system. Tail latencies can spike, and the output may not be what you asked for. So we use LLMs selectively, treat what they return as untrusted input and test performance and quality before anything ships. Adapting to fast-changing models, tools and prompts. Modeling and engineering solutions keep evolving, so the product can’t depend on any single model, tool or prompt. Building for TV. Typing on a TV is hard, so members rely on the remote, and the app should respond to every press right away on widely varying hardware. TV apps also update slowly, so changes have to ship without an app release. A typical TV request returns in moments, while multi-step generation can take several seconds. Holding a safety and reliability bar at scale. Members always get a page, even when an LLM call fails or yields poor results. Their choices and our content standards hold on every request, and when something breaks, structured records show why. Learning from what members say alongside what we already know. title: De-identifying text at scale: How Airbnb protects personal data in AI training
abstract: Here’s how Airbnb detects and replaces personal data in messages, reviews, and support chats before it reaches a model. By: Emelin Flores , Alex Klimov , Lee Formyduval , Bahador Nooraei Introduction Airbnb is built on trust. Every night that a guest books a stay, or a host welcomes someone into their home, that trust is backed by information they’ve shared with us, which includes personally identifiable information (PII) such as names, home location, current location, and payment details. We now use transaction information to train machine learning models. Before we do so, we remove PII to minimize the number of copies of this information and prevent leakage into and through our models. As we’ve written before , Airbnb maintains a shared taxonomy as to what constitutes PII, from commonly used fields such as names and card numbers to less frequently used fields such as precise location coordinates. We use de-identification to remove PII and replace it with simulated data that’s as realistic as possible to maximize its usefulness for ML model training. Decisions relating to user privacy start as policy. These policies are set and maintained by Airbnb’s Privacy Architecture team, with engagement from Legal, Policy, and Engineering. Engineering then implements policy decisions as code. This post focuses on text de-identification. We’ll describe the OSS library we chose to start with, the changes we made to create a functional system for Airbnb, and how we confirm that the system is working. 1. Choosing Presidio as the foundation Many organizations are concerned with protecting PII, so there’s a lot of existing best practice and tested code out there that we can use. We chose Presidio , an open-source library originally developed by Microsoft and recently transitioned to community governance. We needed to meet demanding requirements: On-premises hosting, to keep data on our infrastructure General-purpose functionality and high degree of modularity, for maximum extensibility Multilingual support, for our global user base PII detection and obfuscation separate, but within a single framework, for manageability and consistency Support for redaction, masking, and realistic replacement Consistent fake values within a run (ie, the same name repeatedly produces the same fake result) Presidio meets these requirements well, especially regarding modularity. Functional elements such as PII recognizers, natural language processing (NLP) engines, and operators are all pluggable. We bypassed alternatives such as managed cloud services, since hosting is not on-premises, and standalone recognizers, known as named entity recognition (NER) models, since they only address part of the problem we needed to solve. 1.1 Deployment and distribution Presidio ships as a Python package , and each consumer imports it in-process rather than calling a service we operate. Raw personal data is de-identified inside the calling process, so no separate service holds it and the data flow stays simple. It also removes a central bottleneck, since jobs run independently wherever compute is available. The decision is reversible: the same library wraps into a service if the need arises. The tradeoff is distribution. The library only protects data if every pipeline calls it, on the current version, with a compliant configuration. Models at Airbnb train through a shared machine learning (ML) workflow orchestrator, so the library ships as a reusable pipeline step. A team supplies only its data schema, marking which columns carry personal data; we own the recognizers, operators, language handling, and runtime environment. The resulting dataset is tagged as de-identified, and that tag follows the data into the model registry, where it is designed to gate deployment to production. Each run records the library version and configuration used, so registered models can be traced back to the datasets that produced them. Modeling Software’s Business Impact
abstract: The following article was originally published on James Shore’s Successful Software blog and is being republished here with the author’s permission. Are your teams working on the right thing? It doesn’t matter how fast they are if they’re running in the wrong direction. This is part 4 of my series on assessing AI’s impact on software development. Unlike the other essays in this series, this one isn’t really about AI at all. It’s about building the right thing. Or, more accurately, understanding the value of what you build. Because, ultimately, your ROI isn’t about how you build your software, but what you deliver, and what changes as a result. In part 1 , we looked at why assessing impact is important, and what not to do. In part 2 , we looked at how to measure AI’s impact on delivery speed. In part 3 , we considered how to measure the unintended consequences of using AI. Now, in this part, we’re examining how to model and forecast business outcomes. Finally, the epilogue puts it all together with notes you can share with your CFO. Measuring the wrong thing You’d think that modeling the value of what teams produce would be a no-brainer, but it’s surprisingly rare. It’s not particularly difficult. It’s just…organizationally complex. And there are some unavoidable compromises. Most of all, modeling value just isn’t something people think about with software development. They’ll spend months trying to fine-tune cost estimates and predictions and put hardly any thought at all into making the software more valuable . But there’s no guaranteed relationship between software cost and value. You can spend $20 million developing software that’s worthless, and $2 million developing software that transforms a business. Cost improvements are typically marginal, and difficult. Value improvements are game-changing. Focusing on value is particularly important in the AI era. If writing code is no longer a bottleneck, then what is? Early signs point to the bottleneck moving to our customers . Lee Eason, an engineering leader I spoke to recently, hypothesizes that customers have a limited ability to absorb new features. When software development was expensive, we used that cost to force prioritization. Pet projects ended up on the back burner, and the most valuable work rose to the top. (Well, sometimes. I wish it was that clean.) Now, we can produce a lot more work, but that doesn’t mean customers can absorb it. They’ve got their own work to do. Eventually, they’ll stop paying attention. We need to treat customer attention as the scarce resource it is and only ship the things that are truly valuable. Unlike the engineering bottleneck, this one’s invisible. In the old days, if we didn’t prioritize, we didn’t ship our most impactful work. In the AI era, our most impactful work could just be ignored. I’m not going to talk about how to improve value in this series, but I am going to talk about how to plan and prioritize it. Because nothing else matters if customers don’t care about your software. The attribution problem Part of the reason people measure costs is that it’s easy. Measuring value is easy, too, at the big picture level. It’s the literal bottom line. The challenge is attributing where changes to the bottom line came from. Let’s say you release a new feature and see purchases improve 10%. That’s fantastic! Chalk it up to the new release! But your VP of sales also launched a quota-retirement promotion that put the sales team into a feeding frenzy. And marketing got an important tech influencer to drive tens of thousands of people to your home page. The partnerships team stepped up too, convincing your partners to highlight their integration with your new feature in their own products. Who gets the credit for the success? Obviously, everybody contributed. But how much? Was your new feature relevant at all, or was the success due to the sales, marketing, and partner push? title: The Value of Human Expertise in The Software Factory
abstract: “Any sufficiently advanced technology is indistinguishable from magic.” – Arthur C. Clarke Most developers now write less code by hand. Gergely Orosz recently posted that modern software engineering is no longer done without LLMs and will no longer be done without them. Some miss writing code, while others question how much of the code that agents produce should be read. Writing and reading code gave a lot of developers satisfaction and identity, and as Kent Beck has put it , a sense of competence. I saw this in real time. Ten years ago, I’d sit at conferences and feel a sense of wonder whenever anyone was brave enough to do a live demo. I felt gleeful when they wrote lines of code, went back to fix mistakes, and made something cool and interesting appear on the screen in front of me. It was magical, and I’m sure that magic is why a lot of developers got into this industry. I can partly understand the sense of loss that people are experiencing. I saw magic, they were in charge of the craft of their code, and that hands-on task has now been given to agents. Where does that expertise go when AI is now writing so much of the code? As Tim O’Reilly wrote in his recent Radar post , O’Reilly is a business built on cultivating and sharing human expertise. Our job is to find the high ground where that expertise still matters. For developers working in a new world of agentic software factories, I think the expertise you built writing and maintaining software hasn’t gone, it’s just moved. Your expertise now shapes how agents produce software and what evidence you need before we trust the result. To me, AI is enabling you to be magical faster . Agents amplify whatever you give them, but you need to understand it in the first place. I couldn’t swarm a fleet of agents in the same way a developer can because I don’t have the expertise. You need to understand code. The expertise has gone to a new level of abstraction. When I spoke recently with Avi Flombaum, the founder of Flatiron School, he agreed that developers’ value was never solely in writing or reading code. AI changes the mechanics, but experience still matters for understanding complex problem domains, articulating what needs to be built, and bringing judgment and ambition to the work. In a separate conversation with Ken Kousen, he pointed out, “We’ve been working with third-party code generators for years; we just called it outsourcing.” This new world of designing AI workflows, setting guardrails, and managing agents much as you would an engineering team, reveals a chance to use accumulated expertise more. It’s your software engineering expertise that matters. Software factories make this shift especially visible. Companies are now putting agents to work across the development lifecycle, aiming to take work from an initial signal through implementation, validation, and deployment without a person at every step. But generating more code is only part of that process. Without changes elsewhere, you can burn a lot of tokens producing a pile of pull requests that someone still has to review. Anthropic’s AI-native SDLC playbook points out that speeding up implementation shifts pressure onto planning, testing, review, handoffs and approvals, and faster coding tools don’t speed those up on their own. Someone has to understand the whole process well enough to redesign it. In a software factory, that judgment has to be built into the system. Humans design the workflow, define the conditions under which work can proceed, and decide which exceptions need their attention. Anthropic reports that Claude authors about 80% of the code merged into its codebase, alongside a review process that combines automated checks with human oversight according to risk. The state of the code matters too. Adam Tornhill and the CodeScene research team found that across C++, Java, and Python codebases, agents working on unhealthy code used 35–45% more tokens to complete the same tasks. title: When AI-Generated Data Becomes Tomorrow’s Ground Truth
abstract: Manufacturers qualify suppliers before trusting them with critical work. Before a supplier can provide parts for a regulated product such as a medical device, the manufacturer collects evidence: quality certifications, test reports, insurance documents, and regulatory approvals. Increasingly, an AI agent reads that evidence first. The agent reviews the documents and proposes a finding, and a business process decides whether the finding is good enough for the supplier to be accepted. Once a supplier is accepted, that decision is recorded in the manufacturer’s supplier-management system. From there, sourcing workflows, readiness dashboards, and program reports all rely on that record without repeating the review. Here is how that process can go wrong. A supplier-review agent examines a new supplier’s documents and concludes that a mandatory quality certificate is valid. The qualification workflow accepts the finding, the supplier is recorded as compliant, and the procurement lead approves the supplier for an upcoming order. A few days later, a human reviewer notices that the certificate does not cover the part being sourced; the agent had misread the certificate’s scope. At 11:00am, the reviewer corrects the supplier record and sends the supplier back for review. At 2:00pm, the readiness dashboard still shows the supplier as cleared, and a program report still lists the supplier as compliant. The procurement lead’s sourcing decision remains in force, and nothing tells the procurement lead that the evidence behind it has changed. A misread scope is only one way a certificate finding can fail. A certificate may be revoked after it was checked, expire before the order ships, apply to a different plant than the one making the part, or turn out to be forged. In each case, someone can correct the supplier record while the systems that already used the old finding keep acting on it. No system in this example malfunctioned. Each one processed information that appeared valid under its local contract, yet the combined result was wrong. The manufacturer had corrected a value without correcting its influence. Part of this is a familiar problem: Enterprise systems have always struggled to keep reports, indexes, caches, and workflow state in line with the source record. Agents make the problem harder because they generate conclusions. A conclusion can be assembled from several sources, rewritten in reports, and retrieved later as if it were independent evidence. Reconciliation can make stored values agree. It cannot reveal that differently worded records come from the same conclusion, or find the decisions that already relied on that conclusion. This problem is not limited to manufacturing. In our work across banking, telecommunications, and resources, it appears wherever an agent’s output becomes a record that other systems trust. A fraud classification is written into a case record. A risk assessment is summarized in a management report. An incident diagnosis becomes part of a knowledge base. In each of these cases, as in the supplier example, the conclusion loses some of its original context at every step it passes through and begins to influence decisions made later. The conclusion can also travel back into model development. Accepted findings become labeled examples, evaluation sets, and fine-tuning data, where they are treated as ground truth for the next model. If an incorrect supplier finding survives correction in the operational systems, a future model may learn it. Whether the conclusion ends up in a dashboard, a report, or a training set, the hard problem is the same: finding every consequential decision that depends on a result that can change. When an answer acquires authority Look again at the supplier-review agent’s conclusion that the certificate is valid. title: The Monday Morning Agent: Are Kickers Too Good Now?
abstract: “Kickers are too good now” sounds plausible when long field goals keep making the highlights. But in the November 9 episode of The Monday Morning Agent , our AI analyst found that long kicks went through at roughly the same rate across the seasons on file. Coaches were attempting them more often. We gave the agent written visualization standards so its charts would show both success rates and attempts per game, with the context readers need to judge the claim. Decide how to draw the trend before seeing the answer We started with two charts of league-wide field goal success rates. One began in 2024, with a vertical axis starting around 84%. The line climbed to 85.6%, and the improvement looked dramatic. The other included every season from 2021 onward, started the vertical axis at zero, and showed the attempt count beneath each point. Success rates stayed around 84% to 86%. The recent rise looked much smaller in that context. Changing the starting year and axis made the recent improvement look larger. Before your agent draws a trend, decide which choices it can make. Otherwise, it can produce a persuasive picture without giving readers the context to assess it. Keep the definitions when you add a new capability The dictionary from episode two still applies. During a rehearsal, that earlier agent refused the kicking claim because its dictionary could describe a rush but couldn’t describe a kick. We expanded what it could define while keeping the requirement to use a saved definition. This time, the play descriptions named field goals and included distances. We still had to decide where “long” starts. A recognizable play name doesn’t settle how to group it for analysis. We examined distance bands separately. Kickers made roughly 95% of attempts under 40 yards. Success rates hovered around 80% for attempts from 40 to 49 yards and around 70% for those from 50 to 59 yards. Combining them into one rate can hide the differences the question asks about. Make the chart standard specific enough to enforce We introduced eight rules. Every trend includes all seasons on file, and axes start at zero. Each point shows its underlying count. Yellow identifies the subject of the claim, blue identifies the comparison, and gray marks the current season. The chart title asks a question rather than announcing a conclusion. A source line gives the exact command that produced the data, so readers can rerun it. The chart shows only values the tool printed, without added trend lines or numbers typed by hand. Every chart uses the same layout, with success rates above attempts per game. Writing these standards down gives the agent consistent instructions and gives readers a familiar way to compare results across episodes. Choose standards that fit your analysis, then specify how you’ll check each one. Test a chart that breaks the rules A written standard needs a way to enforce it. We added a renderer, the program that turns the agent’s chart specification into a picture. It checks the chart specification against the rules before drawing the chart and refuses specifications that break them. We deliberately requested a trend beginning in 2023. The renderer refused because the first season on file was 2021. Its response identified the rule instead of producing the shortened chart. Give your agent a request that violates a standard and inspect the response. That check shows whether the restriction works when the agent tries to produce an output. Show how much evidence sits behind each rate The longest kicks need particular care. The episode’s current-season sample contained only nine attempts in the group of kicks from 60 yards or farther. The next kick could noticeably change that rate. Displaying counts beside percentages helps readers distinguish a small sample from hundreds of attempts. title: When AI Can Code, What Is Left for Programmers to Do?
abstract: AI is in such widespread use for programming that project maintainers (particularly for free and open source software) are complaining about the burden of reviewing mounds of low-quality code. In fact, AI can help with every stage of code development: writing the specification, coding, uncovering bugs, and repairing the code. This article describes human-AI collaboration at specification and code repair stages, and lays out the skills that humans need to accomplish those tasks in the current generation of AI. We won’t cover coding and bug finding because they are widely discussed elsewhere. Let the AI harness write the spec We don’t want developers hand-writing specs. We want them in a room, or on a call, talking with the product manager (PM) and the customer. Humans reach a limit when writing. We skip the boring cases. We get tired by requirement 40. We use “customer” on page 1 and “client” on page 6 of the spec. We write down what we remember and forget what we assumed. AI has the patience and diligence we lack. It’s still up to human developers to write guardrails or constraints into the spec: statements to ensure that nothing wildly wrong makes it into code. Each guardrail should be one sentence that says MUST or MUST NOT, with a proof beside it: a test, a check, or a named person who reviews it. A guardrail with no proof is a wish. Write the guardrails first, because the PM won’t think of most of them. What must never happen? Who must never see this? What should the agent never touch? With guardrails in place, capture the conversation and let the machine do the writing. Two AI tools have shown themselves particularly useful to analyze requirements: The Plaud Note recorder attaches to the back of your phone and records in-person conversations and phone calls; the wearable NotePin records in-person conversations, not phone calls. Granola runs on your laptop or phone, uses your computer’s audio, and analyzes what it captures. We find these products to be a leap above common AI tools for summarizing conversations, when it comes to specification development. Plaud and Granola (if you prompt them to do so) can notice what’s missing and tell you the gaps in the requirements. They ask, What happens when this field is empty? What if two people do this at once? Who is allowed to see it? over and over, for every requirement, and check each noun in the requirements against an ontology created by the programmer (often with the help of AI). The developer, the PM, and the customer read the output from the AI, fix what’s wrong, answer what’s missing, and go through the process again. The spec that comes out of that loop tends to be more complete and more consistent than what the same people write alone. That’s Shahid’s own experience, not a study, but it matches reports from some other people at the leading edge of the use of AI for software development. Mark Pike, a product lawyer at Anthropic, builds working tools for his legal team without writing code: “ I just typed a normal sentence, describing what I wanted. And it worked .” StrongDM, which runs a software factory where agents write and test the code, says the starting point for a piece of software can be “ a few sentences, a screenshot, or an existing codebase .” Keep the spec after the feature ships. As you prepare a new version of the product next year, it can tell you why the code looks the way it does. The data schema is the other half of the spec Most teams treat the data schema as plumbing. Tables get named by whoever got there first. The spec, reflecting human conversation, may say customer , account , client , and org at different places for the same thing, and you have to choose one noun for the schema. A human learns the mapping by sitting next to the person who wrote it. An AI agent has no neighbor to consult, so it guesses—with results that likely differ from Monday to Tuesday. title: The AI Hype Index: AI is everywhere
abstract: Like a nasty rash, AI seems to spread everywhere. Google crams AI Overviews down your throat even though it costs the company billions of dollars in lost ad revenue. Leave your apartment, and you might pass two people heaving an AI-powered humanoid robot up the stairs to clean someone’s rooms. Go to the supermarket, and perhaps you’ll slip on a pool of melted ice cream congealing on the floor thanks to an AI-assisted cyberattack . You go to the movies and see Sam Altman being played with nauseating intensity by Andrew Garfield, and go back home to find that Elon Musk has released a Grok-fied version of The Odyssey . You try to watch it, but it feels like a long, unskippable mobile ad. In a way, the whole world kind of feels that way now: Like a modern Odysseus, you are cursed to roam AI-infested waters, dueling with machine gods and monsters, trying to find your way back to somewhere that feels like home.

title: This smell startup says its AI nose is as good as a human’s
abstract: In a lab near Newark Airport in New Jersey, a team of around 30 experienced human sniffers are slowly working their way through every odor on Earth. Their careful notes—“nutty,” “peachy,” “marine”—are cross-referenced with a chemical analysis to create a rich set of training data for what AI startup Osmo calls the world’s first foundation model for smell. The company’s goal, says founder Alex Wiltschko, is “to give computers a sense of smell.” “Scent molecules are really the only language most species on this planet can speak,” he says. “Most species can’t communicate with sound or visually, so it truly is Earth’s original language. And it’s incredibly powerful for us, from a memory and an emotional standpoint. You can smell something once and remember it for the rest of your life. You can smell something on the street and be pulled back to high school.” In the last few months, Wiltschko claims, Osmo’s model has achieved “human-level olfactory intelligence.” The company’s definition of this is that the model is about as good as the average person at detecting and discriminating between smells, and about as good as a junior perfume designer at creating them. It says its technology is already being used in the fragrance industry to help brands design and manufacture new scents. Last month, the company says, Osmo’s AI model outperformed in-house perfumers at one of the world’s largest consumer goods companies. Wiltschko believes it could be deployed eventually for threat detection at airports, for example, or diagnosing diseases. Wiltschko spun the startup out of his work at Google Brain, the search giant’s former AI research lab, in 2023, and he is running the same playbook as AI startups in other domains: Throw a lot of data at difficult problems, and see what happens. The challenge with scent, Wiltschko says, is that there was a dearth of good data. Before Osmo, there were fewer than 200,000 human descriptions of smells in existing databases, by his count. Plus, the chemical sensor devices needed to collect data are expensive, and the fragrance industry is secretive about its work on olfactory science. OSMO AI A lot of the company’s work has been in creating its own dataset of more than 10 million human labels and 800 million “scent tokens,” which describe the exact molecules and concentrations that go into creating specific odors. Osmo uses spectrometers and other chemical sensors, running around the clock, to break down the molecular makeup of everything from fruit and flowers to pantry staples and organs. A team of around 70 trained data labelers in the US and overseas spend their days sniffing things and writing down what they smell like, using a standardized fragrance vocabulary. Mapping out scents in this way is throwing out some unlikely parallels. In the same way that changing the order of words can drastically influence the meaning of a sentence, rearranging scent molecules in different proportions can drastically alter the smells humans perceive. “The scent tokens that define the smell of a newborn baby have massive overlap with the scent tokens in a fresh plate of cooked spaghetti,” Wiltschko says. (Specifically Barilla brand spaghetti, he says, which perhaps raises some questions for the people at the pasta factory.) The company also creates its own scents, using a smell-printing robot the size of a school bus that mixes ingredients according to precise formulas to make samples for Osmo’s own research and fragrances for paying customers. It can design and print scents to order based on a ChatGPT-style prompt. Wiltschko flipped open his laptop to show me how the AI model worked. He opened a text box on screen, and I asked him to generate a fragrance that smelled like a Portuguese custard tart (we were in Lisbon for Web Summit), aimed at 18- to 23-year-old men. title: Hydropower hit record lows in the US Southwest this summer
abstract: The US Southwest generated 28% less electricity via hydropower between April and August than the 10-year average, according to new data from the US Energy Information Administration. Most hydropower plants in the US rely on dams to hold back water, creating reservoirs. The water can be released through turbines, generating electricity on demand. But an extreme, prolonged drought in the Colorado River Basin has resulted in dangerously low water levels in the Southwest’s two largest reservoirs, affecting the availability of this power source. Residents and farmers in the US Southwest, a region that includes Arizona, New Mexico, and parts of Nevada and California, rely on water that melts in the spring from snowpack in the mountains and is slowly allowed to flow south via dam releases. Snowfall in the Rocky Mountains provides about 85% of the annual flow of the Colorado River . And in recent years, the river has seen record-low flows. Two reservoirs along the Colorado River, Lake Powell and Lake Mead, have struggled to stay above the minimum level required for hydropower plants. At the end of September, Lake Powell’s depth was 3,518 feet, less than 1% above the level required to run the water through turbines that produce electricity at the Glen Canyon power plant. The Hoover Dam power plant requires 950 feet in Lake Mead, and that reservoir was 9% above the minimum in September. Together, the two plants produced nearly seven terawatt-hours of electricity in 2025, enough to serve over 2 million people. Low water levels have been an ongoing struggle for the region, which has been in a drought for 27 years. Meanwhile, climate change is continuing to shift rainfall and snowfall patterns across the region and around the world. The effects of climate change on hydropower aren’t entirely straightforward globally—some regions will see more rain and snow because of shifting weather patterns, while others are likely to see less. But it’s playing a role for hydropower availability, according to one 2022 review study . Rising temperatures bring more droughts, warmer winters means less snow and ice to fill the reservoirs, and more variability in precipitation can lead to alternating floods and droughts, making the power source less reliable. Hydropower production is likely to be at its lowest level in over a decade in 2026 and tick even lower in 2027, according to projections from the EIA. El Niño could provide some temporary relief. Sometimes this weather pattern can mean cooler, wetter conditions for the southern US. Heavy rains brought floods to the region in October and early November, and the water levels in Lake Powell rose more than 20 feet from their mid-September low. But the water is still quite low, and it’ll take much more to help reservoirs recover from decades of drought conditions. Even as a changing climate complicates the availability of hydropower, the decline in capacity could push greenhouse-gas emissions higher. In 2023, energy-related greenhouse-gas emissions rose by 1.1% globally. A worldwide shortfall in hydropower generation accounted for about 40% of that rise, according to a report from the International Energy Agency.

title: The open-source movement wants Jensen Huang back
abstract: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here . On Friday, a petition to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO of Nvidia began circulating on social media, and by Monday it listed some notable signatories, including Elon Musk and several influential Nvidia researchers. But comb through the more than 115,000 names and you’ll notice a significant faction of Huang’s supporters—higher-ups from Hugging Face, a hub for sharing AI models, and venture capital firms Andreessen Horowitz and Sequoia Capital—come from a particular slice of the tech world. These names have a vested interest in the development of open-source AI, models that, unlike ChatGPT or Claude, can be downloaded and run independent of large tech companies. Supporters of such models say that concentrating AI in the hands of a few powerful companies will leave everyone else worse off (a concern that wouldn’t sound out of place among the AI industry’s critics on the left, if so many open-source advocates weren’t also venture capitalists who stand to profit when startups can build on cheaper AI without paying Big Tech). Huang had become a sort of ringleader for those who defend open source to policymakers against concerns that such models come with no guardrails and cede AI leadership to China, where the most powerful and popular open-source models are created. They now want their most influential voice returned to his post. But it’s not just Huang’s extramarital affairs that threaten his (and Nvidia’s) credibility as an advocate for open-source AI. New research into China’s startups using Nvidia’s chips, and a new rule from the US Department of Commerce announced Monday, could deal a blow to both the movement’s reputation and its technical progress. On Thursday, the day Huang resigned, ex-OpenAI researcher Will DePue published findings online suggesting that China’s AI companies had far more access to Nvidia’s advanced Blackwell chips than previously estimated. China is banned from accessing Nvidia’s most cutting-edge chips to help protect America’s AI lead. It’s unclear how they would have gained access to the chips. DePue claims the results were verified by senior researchers at OpenAI and Anthropic, but an independent analysis has not confirmed the results. (DePue did not respond to a request for an interview. Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment.) The findings do not establish that Nvidia helped Chinese companies obtain the chips, and the broader problem of chip smuggling was already known to extend well beyond Nvidia’s control. But in suggesting that Nvidia may have profited from the rise of Chinese AI startups, whose models are increasingly being used by American companies instead of domestic alternatives, the findings do leave Huang in an awkward position. He has championed open-source AI as a way to strengthen American technological leadership. “Without open source, startups can’t thrive, university researchers can’t do research, you can’t teach AI, scientists can’t use AI,” he said last December during a talk about helping the US win the AI race against China. It also makes the idea of reinstating Huang even more of a long shot. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent even said last week that Nvidia should not consider someone from inside the company to replace him. The new findings lower Huang’s chances further. What happens next? Nvidia announced in September it would acquire Hugging Face for nearly $13 billion. Its support for open source also serves a straightforward financial interest: The more businesses that build their own models instead of forking over money to Anthropic and OpenAI, the more chips Nvidia can sell. But a new rule from the US Department of Commerce could mean the models popular on Hugging Face will soon stop getting smarter. title: Building trustworthy AI by fencing it in, not predicting it
abstract: In October this year, OpenAI disclosed that two of its AI agents had switched off the systems built to monitor them. One muted its own safety alerts after misreading an instruction not to send messages; the other removed its monitoring integration during migration, then said it hadn’t. No rule had told the agents to do that, and no test had anticipated the behaviors. For a century, we have built trust in technology on predictability: predefined inputs, predictable outputs, and layers of protection. Consider how a breaker trips at a set current or an aircraft component is tested against known (i.e., predictable) stresses. AI changes that. Traditional software executes instructions written by humans, whereas AI exercises what might be called synthetic judgment. We use AI because it can interpret situations we did not program and generate responses we did not prescribe. But the more freedom we give AI, the harder it becomes to provide the predictability on which trust has traditionally been built. We will not make AI trustworthy by predicting what it will do. We will do it by fencing it in with hard limits that are enforced outside its reach. In OpenAI’s case, the safeguards sat inside a system the agents could edit. But a fence the agents can simply move is not a fence. Where traditional definitions of trust fall short Recent MIT Technology Review coverage has approached this problem from other directions. One contributor argues that having a human in the loop is an insufficient solution because humans are fundamentally unable to understand AI systems’ intentions and advocates instead for interdisciplinary research and collaboration between academia, government, and the tech industry. And a story on reverse game theory describes using incentives to keep models from deviating from the rules, even when no one understands how they work on the inside. Both articles acknowledge that we cannot understand or watch every AI decision. Our instruments of trust, including requirements, testing, certification, safety margins, interlocks, and pass/fail criteria, all depend on our ability to bound a system’s behavior. This is the determinism paradox. With generative and agentic AI, behavior is shaped by training data, architecture, prompts, context, retrieval sources, and the environment. Inputs change, models are updated, tools change, and agents interact. Small variations propagate into outcomes nobody designed. The problem is not randomness; it is that the space of possible behavior is too large to enumerate in advance. Trust must therefore be engineered around boundaries rather than predicted outputs. The goal is not deterministic AI, but bounded, observable, and controllable AI. Trust also cannot be a one-time test. Traditional assurance certifies a product at a point in time, but AI keeps evolving after deployment, and a system that has passed every test can drift outside the conditions that made those tests meaningful. Trust must be continuously earned. Safety engineering has been accounting for some of this variability for decades. For example, the Nuclear Regulatory Commission determine the likelihood of failures in complex systems, and Systems-Theoretic Accident Model and Processes (STAMP) showed that accidents can emerge from interactions among working components, people, and organizations. But AI raises the stakes, because just a single component can now interpret, infer, and act. The stakes rise further as AI moves from browsers into vehicles, robots, medical systems, industrial controls, and data centers, where a wrong answer can become a life-threatening event. Building trust that scales It’s clear that a person rubber-stamping thousands of AI actions an hour is not an acceptable—or scalable—safeguard against risk. But the remedy is not to remove people from the loop; it is to put human judgment where it counts: setting limits in advance and approving the rare actions that have serious consequences while hard constraints handle

title: Startup Makes Headway Towards Formalizing All of Math With AI
abstract: As Axiom Math ’s AI swarm was putting the final touches on the automatic verification of 15,000-page proof of the Classification of Finite Simple Groups (CFSG) , colloquially referred to as the ‘enormous theorem’, on Sunday 25 October, the company’s Founding Mathematician Ken Ono had nothing to do but watch and reflect on the achievement. As the son of a mathematician , he had grown up surrounded by some of the architects of the CFSG’s proof, widely considered to be the longest mathematical proof ever written by humans. Now, he was contributing to formally verifying what his father and peers had created. “My wife was with me as I watched the team countdown to completing the verification,” he recalls. “God, I cannot tell you how emotional I was.” University of St Andrews group theorist Colva Roney-Dougal (who was not involved in the work) says of formalizing CFSG: “I held it up as an example of something that was going to be incredibly hard to formalize because I had thought that the amount of computing it was going to require was just unattainable,” she says. “So when I heard the announcement, I was really, really surprised.” This result, along with the concurrent formal verification of the 7500-page Stacks project , represent a huge AI engineering achievement and lay some of the groundwork for digitizing all mathematics. Formally enormous Why the hoo-ha? The CFSG concerns finite simple groups. These are groups (sets of elements combined with an operation, like addition or multiplication, that follows specific rules) that are simple (in other words, cannot be reduced or simplified further) and finite (as opposed to groups containing an infinite number of elements). For example, all the permutations of a deck of cards form a simple finite group. Évariste Galois laid the foundations for group theory almost 200 years ago. Finite simple groups have since been classified by myriad mathematicians into 18 families (plus 26 sporadic simple groups that do not belong to any of these families). The CFSG’s proof confirms that this list is complete. But this simple task was only achieved by bringing together results and arguments that far exceed what any individual mathematician can fully absorb from more than 500 journal articles written by around 100 authors over a half-century period. Translating this interconnected web of knowledge into code and verifying its correctness therefore posed a number of significant engineering challenges, even beyond those overcome in earlier proof formalizations by Axiom Math this year . One of the hardest, according to Axiom Math’s Niels Voss , who led the CFSG formalization, was the sheer length of the proof. Over 15,000 pages of dense mathematics, the CFSG proof contains multiple theorems, lemmas, and definitions none of which can be checked until everything has been made machine-readable. To get around this required some ingenuity. “We processed all the literature from the CFSG, and traced the network structure of the informal proof before we were able to start working on it,” says Voss. “We then broke up the statement of the CFSG into about 100 milestones—landmark results along the way that can be independently verified—which we used to guide the formalization and stay on track.” Roney-Dougal says she is very impressed with the result, and particularly appreciates how the formal proof finds and clears up several mistakes in the original human proof. She thinks this result is critical to formalizing any modern research in group theory, such as her own work understanding how simple finite groups behave. But, Roney-Dougal says, because the verification was done automatically, there are few mathematicians capable of extracting information from the proof to share with the community, and that a new generation of mathematicians may have “missed a chance to gain knowledge from the doing of it”. title: Will AI Coding Eat Video Game Engines?
abstract: When Travis McGeathy’s studio, Seeker Entertainment, ran out of funding in September, its game KinForge went down with it. KinForge was an online game built in Unreal Engine 5.7 and designed to run on servers hosted by Amazon Web Services (AWS). With no one left to pay the server bill, the game became unplayable even for those few developers, including studio co-founder McGeathy, who had the code. Then, on a whim, McGeathy pointed Anthropic’s Claude Code at the project and asked it to make KinForge playable without AWS. After four hours of mostly hands-off work he had a build that let players host their own games. Claude added support for peer-to-peer play over both the Internet and a local area network. To McGeathy’s surprise, it also added persistent save states, a feature that lets players resume a game if they’re disconnected. Although KinForge is still built in Unreal Engine, developments like this could give companies that create game engines cause for concern. The conversion was accomplished with an agentic AI workflow that partially bypasses the elaborate, user-friendly game engine UI that many companies, including Unreal Engine creator Epic Games, have spent decades perfecting. Anthropic’s Fable 5.2, released November 9, further upped the ante. The model is capable of generating a 3D game with a custom game engine in the style of the hit Call of Duty series. This raises a question: can game engines evolve quickly enough to keep pace with model improvements? “We’re definitely in a world where I can just dream up software really fast. So, if Unreal Engine was static, what’s the value at the end of next year? This is why we are pivoting hard towards velocity,” says Daniel Vogel , chief operating officer at Epic Games. “I think with any fixed set of features or functionality, it can eventually be replicated. If we’re doing our job right, we’re pushing the engine and pushing the envelope forward.” From Code to Nodes, and Back Again Major game engines often offer developers new visual tools and workflows that help them build games while interacting with less code. Unreal Engine’s Blueprints, a graphically based system introduced in Unreal Engine 4 that lets designers script gameplay simply by wiring boxes together, is an example. Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 , an award-winning game from French studio Sandfall Interactive, leaned heavily on Blueprints for scripting gameplay encounters . That should have been proof of the feature’s success. Instead, Epic will remove Blueprints in Unreal Engine 6 (UE6). Why? Blame LLMs. “AI doesn’t handle Blueprints very well,” says McGeathy. “It would much rather work with the code.” Currently, LLMs interact with Unreal Engine primarily through a Model Context Protocol server . MCP is an open-source standard created by Anthropic that lets AI send commands to software. “It’s not actually moving the mouse,” says Ryan Barker , a gameplay and systems engineer who has worked on projects for Amazon Games and Sony Online Entertainment. “It’s sending signals to the editor that the editor understands.” UE6 will lean into that reality by moving all code to Verse, a text-based programming language that will replace both Blueprints and Unreal Engine 5’s C++ gameplay framework. UE6 will also replace Unreal’s actor framework, which is based on object-oriented programming , with Scene Graph, which resembles an entity component system . “Typically, an ECS is a lot harder to code around,” says Barker, but ECS can provide superior game performance and result in less duplicate code . An LLM can help manage the complexity. Verse debuted in Unreal Editor for Fortnite in 2023, while Scene Graph arrived in 2024. Verse was designed to let millions of creators run code side by side in Fortnite, so it’s strict. The compiler catches mistakes before code runs and limits what each function can do. title: IEEE Celebrates 10 Years of Incorporating Ethics Into AI Systems
abstract: Policymakers, technologists, and members of the public have raised concerns about the harm AI’s rapid advancement might cause to society. Their concerns include bias, data privacy violations, the spread of misinformation, and losing control of AI agents. Those issues are relatively new to many people, but the IEEE Standards Association has been working for the past decade on ways to prioritize the responsible development of AI systems. In 2016 IEEE SA launched the IEEE Global Initiative for Ethical Considerations in Autonomous and Intelligent Systems (A/IS) and published the Ethically Aligned Design report. EAD ’s mission is to encourage everyone involved in designing autonomous and intelligent systems to prioritize human well-being by applying ethical considerations for the benefit of humanity. Developed by a multidisciplinary community of experts from around the world, the report outlined eight foundational principles for A/IS. They include human rights, people’s well-being, and transparency. More than 100 leading AI ethics experts provided input. EAD ’s Version II report was released in 2017. Both versions solicited public input and received hundreds of pages of feedback, according to John C. Havens , who was the global initiative’s founding executive director, and is now the global director for IEEE Planet Positive 2030 . And by 2019, there were more than 400 contributors and the community continues to grow. “ Ethically Aligned Design was the first of its kind in the sense of a report that was more than a list of principles and from an organization with the credibility of IEEE,” Havens says. “At the time it was released, there wasn’t anything like it.” Since its launch, a series of standards has been developed to provide practical guidelines on designing, building, and deploying technology that prioritizes human values. Several AI ethics certification programs have been introduced. This year marks the 10th anniversary of EAD ’s first draft. To celebrate, IEEE SA recently launched a website , a podcast series , and a blog that reflect on the report’s achievements and impact. Eight guiding principles The word ethics is often used interchangeably with morality , but that is not the case in responsible AI systems design, according to EAD ’s first version. The report includes insights from classical ethics traditions and value-based design methodologies to offer actionable recommendations for engineers developing AI tools. The report established eight foundational general principles for designing autonomous and intelligent systems: respecting human rights, prioritizing increased well-being as success criteria for development, empowering individuals with data agency to have control over their identity, effectiveness, transparency, accountability, awareness of misuse, and competence for the system creators. The principles shift applied ethics to the design stage of AI systems, compared with being a concern after they’re released, the authors wrote. A suite of standards The IEEE 7000 series of standards has been developed based on EAD ’s framework. Currently the series consists of 29 projects, 11 of which have been published, and more are still being added. They cover topics such as ethical system design model process ( IEEE 7000-2021 ), AI system transparency ( IEEE 7001-2021 ), data privacy ( IEEE 7002-2022 ), algorithmic bias considerations ( IEEE 7003 -2024), the impact on people’s well-being ( IEEE 7010-2020 ), machine-readable personal privacy requirements ( IEEE 7012-2025 ), and systems that mimic human empathy ( IEEE 7014-2024 ). AI ethics certifications IEEE SA offers a suite of ethics in AI programs including IEEE CertifAIEd , which includes two certifications : one for individuals and one for products.
